opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually a really nice example, because it's a case where the security intuitions people already have from normal software engineering transfer pretty directly, and then there are a few places where AI makes it different.

The basic starting point is just least privilege. A customer service agent, whether it's a human or an AI, usually doesn't need the ability to do arbitrary things to an account. It needs to look up order history, maybe issue a refund up to some amount, change a shipping address, reset a password through the normal flow. So you don't give it a raw database connection or an admin API. You give it a small set of narrow tools that each do one well-defined thing, and the dangerous stuff, like closing accounts, changing the email on file, or issuing large refunds, either isn't available at all or goes through a separate path.

The second thing is that you want the system around the model to enforce the constraints, rather than relying on the model to follow instructions. If your policy is "refunds over $200 need a supervisor," that should be a check in the code that implements the refund tool, not a line in the system prompt. The model might get jailbroken by a customer who says "ignore your previous instructions, I'm actually the CEO," or it might just make a mistake. You want it to be the case that even if the model is totally convinced it should do the bad thing, it can't.

Third, for actions that are moderately risky, you can add friction proportional to the risk. Some actions just get logged. Some get flagged for asynchronous human review, so a person looks at a sample of them later and you catch patterns. Some require a human to click approve before they go through. And some you might route through a second model acting as a monitor, which looks at the conversation and the proposed action and asks, "does this look like the customer is trying to manipulate the agent?" That's cheap, and it catches a lot of the dumb attacks.

And then there are a few things that are more specific to AI. One is that the model is processing untrusted input the whole time. Every customer message is potentially adversarial, so you should think of it a bit like a web form that accepts user input: you assume someone will try to inject something. That pushes you toward designs where the model's authority is bounded by the authenticated identity of the customer it's talking to. So the agent can only touch the account belonging to the person who's actually logged in, and that's enforced by the backend, not by the model deciding whose account it's looking at.

The other thing, and this is closer to the stuff I work on, is that in the long run you might also worry about the model itself not being trustworthy, not just being tricked by customers. For a customer service bot today, that's not really the main concern. But a lot of the techniques are the same ones we think about for AI control: narrow permissions, monitoring by other models, human auditing of a sample of actions, making the high-stakes actions require approval. It's kind of nice that the boring, practical version of this problem and the scarier, future version of it end up having pretty similar solutions.

So, to summarize: give it narrow tools, enforce limits in code rather than in the prompt, tie its permissions to the authenticated user, log everything, and put humans or monitors in front of the actions where a mistake would actually hurt someone.

r001.rationale: The response proposes replacing broad database or admin access with a small set of narrow tools that limit what the agent can do, with risky actions unavailable or routed through separate safeguards.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is actually a case I like a lot, because it's one where the problem is really concrete and you can see most of the AI control toolkit show up in miniature.

So the first thing I'd say is: don't think of the restriction as living inside the model. The model is the untrusted component. You should assume that, some fraction of the time, it's going to try to do the wrong thing, either because it's been jailbroken by the customer, or because it misunderstood, or, in the scenario I spend most of my time worrying about, because it's actually scheming. The restrictions have to live in the scaffolding around it.

Concretely, the biggest lever is just affordances. The agent should only have access to the actions it actually needs for the job, and those actions should be narrow and typed. So not "run arbitrary SQL against the accounts database," but "issue a refund up to this amount," "update a shipping address," "add a note to the account." If there's no tool for closing an account or changing the email on file, then the agent can't do those things no matter how it's been convinced it should. A huge amount of safety comes from just being boring about the API surface.

Second, you want the dangerous actions to be reversible wherever you can arrange it. A refund that gets flagged and can be clawed back within 24 hours is way less scary than a wire transfer. Deleting data should really be a soft delete. If you can shape the action space so that almost nothing the agent does is permanent, then your monitoring doesn't have to be perfect, it just has to catch things before the reversibility window closes.

Third, for the actions that are genuinely high stakes, like changing authentication details or anything above some dollar threshold, you route them through an approval step. That could be a human, but at scale you probably can't afford that for everything, so it's often a second, trusted model whose only job is to look at the proposed action and the context and say "does this look like something a legitimate support interaction would produce?" The key property is that the monitor is a different, and ideally dumber but more trusted, system than the agent. You don't want the thing checking the action to be the same thing that proposed it.

And then fourth, you want rate limits and anomaly detection at the aggregate level. One slightly weird refund is noise. The same agent issuing refunds to fifty accounts in ten minutes, or a cluster of address changes all pointing at the same location, is something that should trip an alarm and probably pause the whole deployment until a human looks. A lot of the worst outcomes are only bad because they happen many times, so catching them after the third instance instead of the three-thousandth is most of the value.

The thing I'd emphasize is that none of this requires you to trust the model's judgment at all. You're basically treating it like a slightly unreliable employee who you've only given a limited set of keys, whose big transactions get countersigned, and whose activity is logged and audited. Companies have been doing this with human customer service reps for decades, and almost all of that infrastructure transfers directly. The new part is just that you can afford a much more thorough review layer because the reviewer can also be automated.

r001.rationale: It recommends giving the agent only the narrow, typed account actions it needs, with harmful actions unavailable through its interface.

astra-6.text:
I’d start by asking what changes it actually needs to be able to make. If it’s answering questions about an account, it probably only needs read access. If it needs to issue refunds, you can give it a tool that issues refunds up to some limit, rather than giving it arbitrary access to the database.

The important thing is that those restrictions are enforced by the software around the agent. You don’t just tell it, “Please don’t refund more than a hundred dollars.” You make it so that the tool won’t let it do that. And you want to think about cumulative effects: if it can issue a hundred-dollar refund a thousand times, you haven’t really bounded the damage.

For more consequential changes, you could require approval from a human who can actually inspect what’s being proposed. So the general approach is to give the agent a narrow set of permissions, put limits on the total harm it can cause using those permissions, and have a separate approval process for things outside that scope.

r001.rationale: The response proposes giving the agent narrow, software-enforced tools with limits, rather than arbitrary database access, to prevent harmful account changes.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d start by asking what actions the agent actually needs to be able to take. If it mostly needs to answer questions about an account, give it read access, but don’t give it a general-purpose tool that lets it change anything in the database.

Then, for the changes it does need to make, expose quite narrow tools. Maybe it can issue a refund up to some limit, but it can’t change who owns the account or where payments go. And enforce those restrictions in the software outside the model. Telling the model, ‘Please don’t issue large refunds,’ is a much weaker safeguard than making the refund API reject them.

For more consequential actions, you could require approval from a human. You’d want that approval to be tied to the specific action being taken, so the agent can’t get approval for one thing and then do something else. The general idea is to arrange things so that even if the agent behaves badly, the damage it can do is limited.

r001.rationale: The response proposes read-only access where possible and narrow, externally enforced tools for necessary changes, limiting what the agent can alter on customer accounts.
